exact_question: Confirm provisional decision: Donor death, succession, fractional allocations, dormancy, closure and outbound transfers.
original_provisional_answer: Adopt hold-on-notice, suspend-on-verified-death, then activate succession. OD-03: approved unpaid grants proceed unless sponsor policy says otherwise. Dormancy default: 36 months with no advisor activity, then 12 months of outreach on all verified channels and to successors, then a charitable default per the program terms (A4 approval). Closure and outbound transfer follow the state machines in UNB-RCN-ENT-005..007.
jurisdiction: US federal (IRC §4966 ownership/control) plus sponsor program terms; state unclaimed-property law only for uncashed checks

authoritative_findings.claim: A DAF is owned and controlled by the sponsoring organization; advisory privileges are held by the donor or persons the donor appoints, so succession, dormancy and closure rules are matters of the sponsor's program terms, not of the donor's estate.

Fidelity: if no Successor named, balance goes to unrestricted funds on death of last Account Holder; a new Giving Account is created per Successor holding the allocated percentage; if no nominated Successor responds within 90 days the account terminates to unrestricted funds; no testamentary instructions accepted.

Vanguard Charitable: on death or incapacity of one advisor the remaining advisor retains privileges; succession is enacted only when the account is abandoned or on proof of the last advisor's death, incapacity or resignation.
authoritative_findings.pinpoint: Account structure p.3; Enacting a succession plan p.19

authoritative_findings.claim: DAFgiving360: succession activated only upon death or disqualification of all account holders; a new account per successor; executors/trustees cannot exercise privileges unless named successors.
NPT: Legacy Plan activates on written evidence of death of the last primary/joint advisor; six consecutive years without grant recommendations = abandoned, Legacy Plan applies.

Published inactivity triggers range from 2 years (Fidelity Trustee grants after two years without grants), 30 months (Vanguard, DAFgiving360 'inactive'), 30 months + 2 years (DAFgiving360 'dormant' then closure), 36 months (AEF review), 5 years (MS GIFT) to 6 years (NPT).
authoritative_findings.pinpoint: Minimum grant requirements; EV-E-002 Minimum Account Activity; EV-E-003 inactivity; EV-E-004; EV-E-024/025 for AEF, MS GIFT

authoritative_findings.claim: Fidelity: grants to other DAF sponsors do not count as grant activity for its per-account minimum.
authoritative_findings.pinpoint: Minimum grant requirements - Each Giving Account

authoritative_findings.claim: No published sponsor text found addressing whether approved-but-unpaid grants proceed after the recommending advisor's death (OD-03); this remains a sponsor policy choice.

supporting_interpretation: The decided sequence (hold on credible notice, suspend on verified death, then activate succession) matches published practice in substance: every major sponsor activates succession only on proof (death certificate or written evidence) and only after the LAST advisor dies or is disqualified. Fractional successor allocations are standard (Fidelity, NPT, DAFgiving360 open one new account per successor). An approved grant is already the sponsor's decision, so letting it pay after the advisor's death is consistent with the sponsor's exclusive control (interpretation). The 36+12-month dormancy default falls within the published market range (24 months to 6 years).
competing_interpretation: (1) Suspending the whole fund on the death of one joint advisor would contradict Vanguard and DAFgiving360 practice, where surviving advisors keep privileges; suspension should apply to the deceased person's privileges, and fund-level suspension only when the last advisor dies. (2) Some sponsors (Fidelity) act after two years of no grants, so a 48-month path may be looser than a sponsor's own aggregate-payout policy requires; the default must be overridable. (3) A charitable default 'per program terms' must not be the platform's choice: the sponsor's terms determine the destination (own pool, granting history, named charities).
applicability_to_unbound: Unbound must model per-person privilege state separately from fund state, carry per-sponsor configuration (nonresponse window, inactivity thresholds, default destination, successor generation caps, whether testamentary instructions are accepted), and never select a default destination itself.
business_assumptions: Sponsors will configure their own thresholds; Unbound supplies defaults only.
Death verification uses documentary proof (death certificate) as sponsors require.
Escheat analysis (Q11) is limited to uncashed checks; fund balances are sponsor-owned and not unclaimed property of the donor (interpretation).
recommended_answer: Confirm with corrections: (a) Hold on credible notice applies to new advisor-initiated actions; on verified death suspend only the deceased person's privileges; the fund moves to succession only when no living account holder/advisor remains (or all are disqualified). (b) Successor allocations create one new fund per successor by percentage (rounding to the cent, remainder to the first-listed successor unless sponsor rule says otherwise) with a sponsor-configured successor-response window (default 90 days, the Fidelity published value; configurable up to 1 year per JCF); nonresponse routes to the sponsor's configured default. (c) OD-03: approved, unpaid grants proceed unless sponsor policy says otherwise (no published contrary rule found). (d) Dormancy default 36 months no advisor activity + 12 months outreach is acceptable as a configurable default within the 24-month-to-6-year market range; destination always comes from sponsor terms and requires the A4 approval. (e) Closure and outbound transfers per UNB-RCN-ENT-005..007; DAF-to-DAF grants do not count toward activity where the sponsor so specifies.
remaining_uncertainty: Individual sponsors' unpublished operating procedures; treatment of approved grants after death at sponsors that have not published a rule; state probate claims by estates (none found that override sponsor ownership).
consequences_if_wrong: Wrong fund-level suspension would freeze surviving joint advisors (customer harm, complaints); wrong default destination would breach sponsor terms and could misdirect charitable assets.
conservative_fallback: If sponsor has not configured a rule: suspend the deceased person's privileges, hold the fund's new grant intake pending sponsor review, and route any disposition to a sponsor approver (no automatic default).
alternative_design: Parameter-only design (no default dormancy disposition; every dormancy closure is a sponsor-approved task) - lowest exposure, higher sponsor workload (~1 manual review per dormant fund), no lost capability. Versus configurable default with A4 approval (recommended): low exposure, low friction.
required_acceptance_criteria: Given a fund with two advisors, When a verified death certificate for one is recorded, Then only that person's privileges are suspended and the surviving advisor can still recommend grants.

Given the last advisor's death is verified, When succession activates with successors at 50/30/20%, Then three new funds are created whose balances sum exactly to the source balance and the remainder cent rule is logged.
Given a named successor does not respond within the sponsor-configured window, Then the fund routes to the sponsor's configured default and requires sponsor approval before any distribution.
Given a grant was approved before death notice, When death is verified, Then the grant pays unless the sponsor policy flag 'cancel_approved_on_death' is true.

Given a fund has no advisor activity for the configured inactivity period, Then outreach starts on all verified channels and to successors, and no disposition occurs before the outreach period ends and an A4 approval is recorded.
Given a sponsor marks testamentary instructions as not accepted, When an executor submits a will-based instruction, Then the platform rejects it with a reason and records the document.
reconsideration_triggers: A sponsor publishes rules on approved grants after death
State legislation treating DAF advisory rights as estate property
Change in a sponsor's published inactivity thresholds
external_authorization_required: Each sponsor's board- or management-approved program terms (succession, dormancy, default destination) loaded as configuration; no other external authorization identified.

corrections_to_prior_records.issue: Reads as fund-level suspension on any death; published sponsor practice (Vanguard, DAFgiving360, NPT) keeps surviving advisors' privileges and activates succession only when the last advisor dies or is disqualified.
corrections_to_prior_records.correction: Suspend the deceased person's privileges; fund-level succession only when no living account holder remains.

corrections_to_prior_records.record_or_artifact: RCD-022 validation_required ('counsel on escheat of balances (Q11)')
corrections_to_prior_records.issue: Fund balances are owned by the sponsor (§4966(d)(2)(A)(ii)); escheat analysis concerns uncashed grant checks, not dormant fund balances.
corrections_to_prior_records.correction: Limit Q11 escheat validation to uncashed/voided checks; dormant balances follow sponsor program terms.

Vanguard Jan 2026: inactive after 30 months; minimum one $500 grant every three years.

exact_question: Confirm provisional decision: Can an agent under POA, guardian or conservator exercise DAF advisory privileges?
original_provisional_answer: An agent under a power of attorney may exercise advisory privileges only if the instrument expressly grants authority to make gifts or charitable donations, the sponsor's program terms allow representatives, and the instrument is verified. Guardians and conservators act only under a court order that covers charitable gifts. Otherwise the privileges are suspended pending succession or court order.
jurisdiction: State law (UPOAA in roughly 26-30 states; non-uniform POA statutes elsewhere, e.g. FL, NY, CA); state guardianship/conservatorship law (UGCOPAA enactments, older UGPPA); federal §4966 for DAF definition

authoritative_findings.claim: UPOAA §201(a): an agent may make a gift on behalf of the principal or with the principal's property only if the POA expressly grants that authority AND exercise is not otherwise prohibited by another agreement or instrument to which the authority or property is subject.

UPOAA §120: a person presented with an acknowledged POA must accept it or request certification/translation/opinion within seven business days unless a refusal ground applies (e.g., not otherwise required to transact with the principal in the same circumstances; good-faith belief agent lacks authority; APS report); wrongful refusal risks a court order and fees.
NC enactment varies the uniform text: general gift authority reaches charitable gifts only 'in accordance with the principal's history of making or joining in the making of gifts'.
Conservators need specific court authorization, after notice, to make non-de-minimis gifts (UGCOPAA enactment, Maine).
DAF assets are owned and controlled by the sponsor; advisory privileges arise from donor status or donor appointment, so a DAF grant recommendation is not a gift of the principal's property.
Vanguard accepts a copy of a durable POA as written proof of the advisor's incapacity, which triggers the succession plan rather than conferring privileges on the agent.
authoritative_findings.pinpoint: Account structure 'Successor advisor'; Enacting a succession plan

authoritative_findings.claim: DAFgiving360: an executor or trustee cannot exercise account privileges unless also a named successor; Fidelity: only Account Holders and Authorized Persons designated by an Account Holder exercise privileges, and Fidelity may decline or revoke any designation.
authoritative_findings.pinpoint: p.31 n.14; EV-E-001 'Fidelity Charitable approval', 'Authorized Person'

authoritative_findings.claim: Proposed regs would treat any person appointed or designated by a donor, with no particular form, as a donor-advisor (relevant to §4967/§4958 status of agents) - proposed only, not effective as of 2026-11-24.

supporting_interpretation: Because the sponsor owns the assets and the privilege is contractual, the governing question is what the program terms allow. UPOAA §201(a) itself defers to 'another agreement ... to which the authority ... is subject', so sponsor terms that limit representative authority are effective in UPOAA states. Requiring express gift/charitable authority is a sound proxy for the principal's intent, but the strictly legal hook is the program terms. A sponsor that never accepts agents (only donor-designated Authorized Persons) is consistent with Fidelity, DAFgiving360 and Vanguard practice.
competing_interpretation: An agent with broad general authority could argue that recommending grants from a DAF is not a 'gift' (the gift was made at contribution) and so does not need express gift authority; and UPOAA §120 could be read to require the sponsor to accept an acknowledged POA within 7 business days. Counter: §120(b)(1) excuses acceptance where the person is not otherwise required to transact with the principal in the same circumstances; the sponsor never must act on a recommendation. The sponsor's terms should say expressly that agents act only as the program allows. States outside UPOAA (e.g., Florida §709.2202 requires principal's signature/initials next to gift powers - recalled, not fetched) can be stricter.
applicability_to_unbound: Unbound should implement a representative-authority record (instrument type, jurisdiction, acknowledgment, scope flags incl. express gift/charitable authority, court order scope, expiry) and a 7-business-day POA response clock with statutory refusal-reason codes, while the sponsor's terms decide whether agents may act at all.
business_assumptions: Sponsor program terms will state whether agents, guardians and conservators may exercise privileges.
Sponsors will want to avoid UPOAA §120 refusal liability by responding within 7 business days with a documented ground.
recommended_answer: Confirm with refinements: (1) Default: an agent under a POA may exercise advisory privileges only if (a) the sponsor's program terms permit representatives, (b) the instrument is acknowledged and verified, and (c) it expressly grants authority to make gifts or charitable donations (or expressly references the DAF/advisory privileges); exercise must follow the principal's giving history and may not benefit the agent. Contributions by an agent always require express gift authority (UPOAA §§201, 217). (2) Guardians of the person have no authority; conservators act only under a court order specifically authorizing charitable gifts or DAF advisory acts. (3) Otherwise treat the POA/court order as evidence of incapacity, suspend the principal's privileges, and activate the next named advisor/successor per program terms (Vanguard pattern). (4) Respond to any presented POA within 7 business days (accept, request certification, or refuse with a §120 ground) and log it. (5) The agent's acts are logged as the agent's, and the agent is treated as a donor-advisor for impermissible-benefit screening.
remaining_uncertainty: No case law or IRS guidance found on agents exercising DAF advisory privileges; state variations (non-UPOAA states, NC-style charitable-history limits, Florida execution formalities) not fully surveyed.
consequences_if_wrong: Accepting an agent without authority could facilitate elder exploitation and expose the sponsor to claims; refusing without a statutory ground in a UPOAA state could bring a court order and fee award.
conservative_fallback: Program terms state that representatives may not exercise advisory privileges; POAs and court orders are used only to verify incapacity and trigger succession; respond within 7 business days citing §120(b)(1)-type ground.
alternative_design: (A) Donor-designated Authorized Person/interested-party roles set while the donor has capacity (Fidelity/Vanguard pattern) instead of accepting POAs: lowest exposure, modest friction (donor must act in advance), small lost opportunity for incapacitated donors without designees. (B) Accept agents with express authority (recommended default): medium exposure, needs instrument review (~30 min per case). (C) Accept any general POA: highest exposure; rejected.
required_acceptance_criteria: Given an acknowledged POA is uploaded, When 7 business days elapse without a decision, Then the case escalates and the clock state is visible to the sponsor.
Given a POA without express gift or charitable authority, When the agent recommends a grant, Then the recommendation is blocked with reason code REPRESENTATIVE_AUTHORITY_INSUFFICIENT.
Given a conservator presents letters without a court order authorizing gifts, Then advisory privileges are suspended and succession/next-advisor routing is offered.
Given an agent-recommended grant would benefit the agent or their dependants, Then it is blocked and routed to compliance.
Given sponsor terms disallow representatives, When any POA is presented, Then the platform records a refusal citing the program-terms ground within 7 business days.
reconsideration_triggers: Court decision on agents and DAF privileges
Sponsor operates in a non-UPOAA state with mandatory acceptance rules
SR-style statutory changes to POA acceptance periods
external_authorization_required: Sponsor program-terms clause on representatives approved by the sponsor; for conservators, a court order specifically authorizing the act.

related_question_answers.answer: Only where sponsor terms allow representatives and a verified, acknowledged instrument expressly grants gift/charitable authority; record instrument, scope, expiry and sponsor acceptance; a generic POA confers no authority; respond within 7 business days (UPOAA §120).

corrections_to_prior_records.record_or_artifact: XID-TRS-001 decision_outcome.authority ('Uniform Power of Attorney Act §201 (general knowledge)')
corrections_to_prior_records.issue: Cited from general knowledge; also omits that §201(a) defers to other agreements governing the authority and omits the §120 seven-business-day acceptance duty.
corrections_to_prior_records.correction: Cite UPOAA §§119, 120, 201(a), 217 (fetched) and state enactments; add 7-business-day response clock and refusal-ground logging.

corrections_to_prior_records.issue: Implies the gift-authority rule directly governs DAF grant recommendations; DAF assets are sponsor-owned, so the controlling rule is the sponsor's program terms (interpretation).
corrections_to_prior_records.correction: State that program terms govern; express gift authority is the required evidential threshold, mandatory for contributions by agents.

landscape_update_candidates: DAFgiving360 2024 policies: executors/trustees cannot exercise privileges unless named successors (n.14 p.31).

exact_question: Confirm provisional decision: Legal basis, maximum duration and liability for protective suspension of a representative.
original_provisional_answer: The sponsor may place a protective suspension on a representative's advisory privileges when it reasonably believes exploitation or abuse of authority is occurring. Maximum 15 business days, one extension of up to 10 business days by an independent reviewer, then referral to counsel or the appropriate authority. No money moves during suspension; the principal is notified unless notice would put them at risk.
jurisdiction: Sponsor program terms (contract); federal §4966 control; FINRA 2165 and Senior Safe Act as analogies only; state APS reporting laws vary

authoritative_findings.claim: Sponsors reserve the right to limit, suspend or revoke privileges in their sole discretion and to freeze accounts while an advisor is under investigation or subject to court orders.
authoritative_findings.pinpoint: Termination of account privileges; EV-E-003 Account privilege limitations; EV-E-001 'Termination of Giving Account privileges'

authoritative_findings.claim: FINRA Rule 2165 permits holds on disbursements and securities transactions where exploitation of a Specified Adult is reasonably believed: 15 business days, +10 after internal review, +30 more if reported to a state regulator/agency or court; notice within 2 business days except to suspected parties.
The 30-business-day extension took effect 2022-03-17; a further amendment filing SR-FINRA-2026-018 is pending.

Senior Safe Act gives immunity for good-faith reports to APS/regulators/law enforcement only to listed covered financial institutions and trained employees; it authorizes no holds; a DAF sponsor is not a listed institution.
UPOAA §120(b)(6) lets a person refuse an acknowledged POA if it reports, or knows another has reported, suspected exploitation by the agent to APS.
Because the sponsor has exclusive legal control and privileges are contractual, a time-bounded protective suspension needs no statutory safe harbor; its legal basis is the program terms.

supporting_interpretation: The legal basis is contractual: published terms of Fidelity, Vanguard and DAFgiving360 already allow suspension in sole discretion with no time limit. A short, reviewed time limit is a self-imposed fairness control, not a legal requirement; FINRA 2165 is a sound template because it pairs a reasonable-belief trigger with notice, internal review and escalation.
competing_interpretation: A fixed 15+10 business-day cap could force release before an APS or court process completes; FINRA itself allows a further 30 business days once reported to a regulator or court. Conversely, an indefinite freeze without review may be criticized as unfair to a legitimate representative, though sponsor terms permit it.
applicability_to_unbound: Platform implements the hold, clocks, reviewer roles, notice templates and escalation; the sponsor decides. The platform must never auto-release a hold that has been escalated to APS, law enforcement or a court.
business_assumptions: Sponsors adopt program-terms language permitting protective suspension of representatives.
No money moves during suspension except sponsor-approved protective actions.
Sponsors may voluntarily report to APS; immunity depends on state APS law, not the Senior Safe Act.
recommended_answer: Confirm with amendments: legal basis = sponsor program terms (exclusive legal control), not statute. Trigger: reasonable belief of exploitation or abuse of authority. Initial suspension up to 15 business days; one extension up to 10 business days after documented independent review; a further extension up to 30 business days (or until resolution) only when the matter has been reported to APS, law enforcement, a regulator or a court, or a court/agency directs. Notice to the principal and other authorized parties within 2 business days unless they are suspected or notice would put the principal at risk. On expiry without escalation: release or convert to a sponsor revocation decision - never silent lapse. Liability: rely on program-terms sole-discretion and exculpation clauses; no federal immunity applies to sponsors.
remaining_uncertainty: State APS reporting/immunity statutes for charities not surveyed; no case law on DAF representative suspensions found; pending SR-FINRA-2026-018 may change the analogy.
consequences_if_wrong: Too-short limits could release funds to an exploiter; too-long or unreviewed holds could prompt complaints or claims by legitimate representatives.
conservative_fallback: Program terms allow indefinite suspension at sponsor discretion with mandatory 15-business-day reviews and recorded reasons.
alternative_design: Rely only on donor-pre-designated trusted contact and refuse representatives (see XID-TRS-001 option A): avoids most exploitation exposure; friction for families; loses ability to serve incapacitated donors through agents.
required_acceptance_criteria: Given a protective suspension is placed, Then a 15-business-day expiry is set and the principal is notified within 2 business days unless the 'notice_risk' flag is set with a reason.
Given an independent reviewer extends, Then the total cannot exceed 25 business days unless an escalation record (APS, law enforcement, regulator or court) exists.
Given an escalation record exists, Then a further extension up to 30 business days or until a court/agency directs is permitted and the hold cannot auto-release.
Given a suspension is active, Then no grant, transfer or privilege change by the representative is executed.
Given expiry is reached without decision, Then the case escalates to the sponsor owner rather than releasing silently.
reconsideration_triggers: State legislation extending exploitation-hold safe harbors to charities
external_authorization_required: Sponsor approval of program-terms wording for protective suspension.

related_question_answers.answer: Legal basis is the sponsor's program terms under its exclusive legal control; max 15 business days + 10 on independent review, + up to 30 more only after report to APS/law enforcement/regulator/court; documented authority, reason, owner, review deadline and escalation; never auto-release a legally required or escalated hold.

corrections_to_prior_records.record_or_artifact: XID-CLM-002 decision_outcome.authority ('FINRA Rule 2165 temporary hold: 15 business days, extendable 10')
corrections_to_prior_records.issue: Incomplete: since 2022-03-17 Rule 2165 allows a further 30 business days when reported to a state regulator/agency or court, and covers securities transactions as well as disbursements; a further amendment (SR-FINRA-2026-018) is pending.
corrections_to_prior_records.correction: Model 15 + 10 + 30 (escalated) business days, as an analogy only.

landscape_update_candidates: Vanguard (2026) and DAFgiving360 (2024) terms: may freeze an account while an advisor is under investigation by authorities.

exact_question: Confirm provisional decision: Approve the public decline reason catalog and neutral codes.
original_provisional_answer: Adopt a public decline reason catalog of neutral codes: ELIGIBILITY_NOT_CONFIRMED, ORGANIZATION_STATUS_CHANGED, PURPOSE_NOT_PERMITTED_BY_POLICY, IMPERMISSIBLE_BENEFIT, INFORMATION_NOT_RECEIVED, PAYMENT_DETAILS_UNVERIFIED, COMPLIANCE_REVIEW (restricted reasons, e.g. sanctions or investigations, always map here), FUND_BALANCE_INSUFFICIENT, DUPLICATE_REQUEST, SPONSOR_DISCRETION. Free-text explanations are optional and reviewed.
jurisdiction: US; sponsor program terms; state defamation law (qualified privilege); no federal adverse-action rule applies to DAF grant declines

authoritative_findings.claim: Sponsors retain sole discretion over grants and may decline recommendations; DAFgiving360 notifies account holders when it declines a recommendation because a charity did not supply information within 30 days.
Fidelity may remove an organization from eligibility and limit privileges in its sole discretion; no published obligation to state reasons.
authoritative_findings.pinpoint: Remedial actions; Timing of grant review

authoritative_findings.claim: No statute or IRS guidance found that requires a DAF sponsor to give a reason for declining a grant recommendation; ECOA/Reg B and NAIC Model 900 adverse-action rules do not apply to DAF grants (interpretation; cited as analogies only).
Statements about third parties (charities) shared with an interested person without malice are conditionally privileged in California; the privilege is lost on malice.

supporting_interpretation: Neutral codes that describe the sponsor's decision rather than assert facts about a charity reduce defamation exposure (truthful, non-accusatory) and avoid disclosing sanctions screening or investigations. Codes like ORGANIZATION_STATUS_CHANGED reflect public IRS data and are verifiable.
competing_interpretation: IMPERMISSIBLE_BENEFIT shown to a donor implies wrongdoing by the donor (not the charity) - acceptable because it concerns the donor's own recommendation, but wording should describe the rule ('Grant would provide a benefit not permitted by policy'). SPONSOR_DISCRETION and COMPLIANCE_REVIEW are opaque; donors may perceive unfairness, but no law requires more.
applicability_to_unbound: Platform ships the catalog as sponsor-configurable defaults with fixed mapping of restricted internal reasons to COMPLIANCE_REVIEW; free text gated by sponsor review.
business_assumptions: Sponsors accept a shared neutral code set.
Restricted reasons (sanctions, investigations, law-enforcement requests) never surface in donor- or charity-facing text.
recommended_answer: Approve the 10-code catalog as sponsor-configurable defaults with: (1) donor-facing text that describes the policy outcome, not facts about a charity (e.g., PURPOSE_NOT_PERMITTED_BY_POLICY, not 'charity engaged in X'); (2) mandatory mapping of sanctions, investigation, and law-enforcement reasons to COMPLIANCE_REVIEW; (3) charity-facing communications limited to status codes; (4) free text optional, reviewed, and drawn from approved phrases; (5) an appeal/reconsideration path per UNB-XIN-CLM-001. This is a business policy; no legal reason-giving duty was found.
remaining_uncertainty: State consumer-protection theories (unfair practices) against opaque declines untested; counsel wording review still prudent but not a legal gate.
consequences_if_wrong: Accusatory free text could create defamation claims by charities; revealing sanctions screening could compromise investigations.
conservative_fallback: Disable free text; show only the code label.
alternative_design: Single generic 'Not approved' with private reason: lowest legal exposure, highest donor friction and support cost; loses actionable feedback.
required_acceptance_criteria: Given a decline with an internal sanctions or investigation reason, Then the external code is COMPLIANCE_REVIEW and no internal reason text is exposed via UI, API, email or export.
Given free text is entered, Then it cannot be released until a second reviewer approves it.
Given a charity-facing message, Then it contains only status codes and no donor-identifying or investigation content.
reconsideration_triggers: Regulation requiring reason-giving for DAF declines
Defamation claim or complaint involving decline text

corrections_to_prior_records.issue: NAIC Model 900 governs insurance adverse underwriting decisions and does not apply to DAF sponsors; not verified in this pass.
corrections_to_prior_records.correction: Label it an analogy; the decision rests on sponsor discretion (program terms), not on any reason-giving duty.

exact_question: Confirm provisional decision: Confidential sponsor investigations versus propagation of adverse charity findings.
original_provisional_answer: Propagate holds and verified public-source facts to every affected sponsor; never propagate sponsor-private investigation content.
jurisdiction: US; state defamation/qualified-privilege law (varies); IRS reliance rules

authoritative_findings.claim: Grantors may not rely on IRS listings if they knew of, were aware of imminent, or were partly responsible for, a revocation; knowledge received from other sponsors could defeat reliance for the receiving sponsor.
Communications without malice to an interested person by one also interested are conditionally privileged (California).
Sponsors treat investigations of account holders as grounds to freeze accounts, showing investigation information is sponsor-held and sensitive.

supporting_interpretation: Propagating verified public-source facts (IRS revocation, Pub 78 removal, OFAC listing, court judgments) is low risk: truth and public-record status defeat defamation, and common-interest privilege covers communications among sponsors with pending grants to the charity. Sponsor-private investigation content is unverified opinion and confidential sponsor data; propagating it risks defamation (privilege lost if malice or excessive publication) and breaches multi-tenant confidentiality.
competing_interpretation: Rev. Proc. 2018-32 §4.04 suggests that when one sponsor learns of facts showing imminent revocation, other sponsors' reliance could be affected if they are told; withholding risk signals could leave other sponsors exposed. Also, coordinated declines among sponsors could raise group-boycott (antitrust) questions (interpretation; not researched).
applicability_to_unbound: The platform is the conduit; it should propagate system holds tied to public facts and a neutral 'review requested' signal, never another tenant's private evidence.
business_assumptions: Sponsors are separate tenants with contractual confidentiality.
Public facts are re-verified independently from the source before propagation (SPD-GRT-002).
recommended_answer: Confirm: propagate (a) holds that derive from verified public facts (IRS revocation/auto-revocation, Pub 78 removal, OFAC SDN match, published court judgments) with source and retrieval timestamp, re-verified by the platform from the primary source; (b) never propagate sponsor-private investigation content, suspicions or decisions; (c) optionally allow a sponsor to share an anonymised, neutral 'enhanced review recommended' flag only under a written inter-sponsor information-sharing agreement that recites the common interest, limits recipients to sponsors with pending or recent grants to the charity, and contains no factual allegations.
remaining_uncertainty: Qualified privilege rules differ by state; antitrust exposure of coordinated declines not researched; no case law on DAF sponsor information sharing found.
consequences_if_wrong: Propagating private allegations could bring defamation and confidentiality claims; failing to propagate public facts could lead to taxable distributions or grants to revoked charities.
conservative_fallback: Propagate only public-source facts; no inter-sponsor flags at all.
alternative_design: Each sponsor sees only primary-source public data refreshed by the platform (no sponsor-originated signals): minimal legal exposure, loses early-warning value.
required_acceptance_criteria: Given sponsor A records an internal investigation note on a charity, Then no field of that note is visible to sponsor B via UI, API, export or logs.
Given the IRS auto-revocation list adds a charity, Then a hold is placed for every sponsor with open grants to it, citing the IRS source and retrieval time.
Given a public fact is reported by a sponsor, Then it propagates only after the platform re-verifies it from the primary source.
reconsideration_triggers: Antitrust guidance on charitable sector coordination
external_authorization_required: Written inter-sponsor information-sharing agreement only if the optional neutral flag is enabled.

exact_question: Confirm provisional decision: What charity-status freshness and deep-review intervals apply, and can cross-sponsor evidence be relied on?
original_provisional_answer: Adopt RR-REQ-X-007-r1. An IRS-status check happens at approval and again at payment release, using an observation retrieved within the last 24 hours from the latest published TEOS/BMF/auto-revocation revision, with a per-sponsor snapshot. Deep review defaults to every 180 days (sponsor may tighten, not loosen), with automatic refresh starting 30 days before expiry. Cross-sponsor evidence may be reused as input only.

authoritative_findings.claim: TEOS/Pub 78 data, the EO BMF extract and the Auto-Revocation List are each 'generally updated monthly'.
IRS page states bulk data files are updated monthly; on 2026-11-24 Pub 78 and auto-revocation files were last updated 2026-11-11 and EO BMF 2026-11-10.

Sponsoring organizations may rely on listed public charity status for §4966 grantmaking; reliance continues until public announcement (or auto-revocation posting) unless the grantor knew, was aware of imminent revocation, or was partly responsible.
Reliance applies only to grants made in the organization's official/recognized name and not to group-exemption subordinates.
No IRS rule prescribes a 180-day deep-review interval or a 24-hour data freshness window; these are business controls.

supporting_interpretation: Because IRS data change only about monthly, a check at approval and again at release against the latest published file suffices to obtain Rev. Proc. 2018-32 reliance; the 24-hour retrieval window ensures the newest monthly release is used. Reliance is per grant date, so a release-time check matters most.
competing_interpretation: A 24-hour window adds operational dependency for little legal gain; checking that the snapshot equals the latest IRS posting (by posting date) is the legally meaningful test. Cross-sponsor evidence: reliance is defeated by knowledge, so a sponsor that receives an adverse public fact via the platform loses reliance for later grants - propagation is therefore protective.
applicability_to_unbound: Implement the freshness test as 'snapshot built from the most recent IRS posting (posting-date check) and retrieved within 24h'; store posting date, retrieval time and EIN/name match with each grant.
business_assumptions: The platform ingests monthly IRS files promptly after posting.
Sponsors accept 180-day deep review as a default.
recommended_answer: Confirm with clarification: status check at approval and at release against the latest published TEOS/Pub 78, EO BMF and Auto-Revocation releases (record posting date; retrieval within 24h is an operational target, not a legal threshold); grant made to the listed legal/recognized name; group-exemption subordinates flagged for additional verification; deep review default 180 days (sponsor may tighten) with refresh 30 days before expiry; cross-sponsor evidence reused only as input, with any known adverse public fact always considered (knowledge defeats reliance).
remaining_uncertainty: The 180-day interval is a business choice with no legal source; IRS could change publication cadence.
consequences_if_wrong: Stale data could produce grants to revoked organizations; if sponsor knew, reliance fails and §4966 tax could apply.
conservative_fallback: Block release if the latest IRS posting date is newer than the snapshot's source date.
alternative_design: Live third-party verification API (e.g., Candid) at release: higher cost and vendor dependency, marginal freshness gain since IRS data are monthly.
required_acceptance_criteria: Given the IRS posts a new monthly file, When a grant is released, Then the status check uses a snapshot built from that posting and records its posting date.
Given a charity appears on the Auto-Revocation List, Then pending releases to it are held for all sponsors.
Given a recipient is a group-exemption subordinate, Then the record is flagged 'reliance not available under Rev. Proc. 2018-32 §6.03'.
reconsideration_triggers: New revenue procedure superseding Rev. Proc. 2018-32

related_question_answers.answer: Share independently verified public facts (re-fetched from IRS/OFAC sources) across sponsors; never share private evidence or approval decisions; known adverse public facts defeat Rev. Proc. 2018-32 reliance, so they should propagate.
Only after the platform independently re-verifies the fact from a primary source; the sponsor-originated correction is a lead, not evidence.
Propagate holds and verified public-source facts; never propagate sponsor-private investigation content (see RCD-029 dossier).

corrections_to_prior_records.issue: Correct that 180 days is not a legal standard, but the stated basis should be that reliance is tied to IRS publication/announcement dates (Rev. Proc. 2018-32 §§4-5), with data updated monthly.

exact_question: Confirm provisional decision: In a distribution-partner exit, may the original sponsor approve outbound transfer grants by a batch policy, and may it decline or impose conditions?
original_provisional_answer: In a partner exit the original sponsor may adopt a written exit policy as the exercise of its discretion. The policy is applied per fund: each transfer is a separate decision with its own record citing the policy, hold and sanctions checks. The sponsor may decline or condition individual transfers (open holds, sanctions matches, expenditure-responsibility grants outstanding, unresolved disputes). A contractual pre-commitment to transfer that removes sponsor discretion is not permitted.
jurisdiction: US federal (§4966); sponsor program terms; state charity law for large asset transfers

authoritative_findings.claim: A distribution from a DAF to any other DAF, or to a 170(b)(1)(A) public charity (including another sponsor), is not a taxable distribution.
The DAF is owned and controlled by the sponsor; a binding pre-commitment to transfer could undercut 'owned and controlled' (interpretation).
Proposed regs would treat a series of distributions under a plan inconsistent with §4966 as one distribution - proposed only.

Fidelity acknowledges grants to other DAF sponsors (excluded from its activity test); NCF bars succession funds from transferring to other sponsors; no sponsor publishes an outbound-transfer procedure or fee.
Transfers over 25% of net assets that are not ordinary-course grants are reported on Schedule N Part II.

supporting_interpretation: A written exit policy adopted by the sponsor's board or authorized officer is itself an exercise of the sponsor's discretion; applying it per fund with individual decision records preserves control and creates an audit trail. Declining or conditioning transfers for open holds, sanctions, ER grants outstanding, or disputes is within sponsor discretion.
competing_interpretation: If the partner agreement obliges the sponsor to transfer on exit, the commitment may be read as donor or third-party control over DAF assets; also, fees or delays imposed to discourage exit are lawful contractually but may attract reputational/regulatory scrutiny.
applicability_to_unbound: Unbound generates batch recommendations and per-fund decision records; executes only after a recorded sponsor approval per fund (or per policy with each fund's checks passed and logged).
business_assumptions: Distribution-partner agreements will contain no mandatory transfer clause.
Receiving sponsors are verified 170(b)(1)(A) organizations.
recommended_answer: Confirm: sponsor adopts a written exit policy (by its board or delegated officer) as its discretionary decision; Unbound applies it fund by fund, each with its own record citing the policy, eligibility, sanctions and hold checks; sponsor may decline or condition individual transfers; no contractual pre-commitment that removes discretion. Fees and deadlines: lawful if disclosed in program terms; no legal restriction found, but avoid terms that make transfer effectively impossible. If the exit moves >25% of sponsor net assets, flag Schedule N reporting.
remaining_uncertainty: No IRS guidance on batch-policy approvals; final §4966 regulations could add anti-abuse rules.
consequences_if_wrong: Loss of exclusive-control posture; disputes with exiting partners.
conservative_fallback: Per-fund manual approval by a sponsor officer.
alternative_design: Per-fund manual approval: zero ambiguity, high labor (minutes per fund x thousands). Batch policy + per-fund automated checks + officer sign-off of the batch list (recommended): low labor, same control evidence.
required_acceptance_criteria: Given an exit policy is approved, When a batch runs, Then each fund produces an individual decision record with policy ID, checks and outcome.
Given a fund has an open hold, sanctions match, outstanding ER grant or dispute, Then it is excluded from the batch and routed for individual decision.
Given a partner contract contains a mandatory-transfer clause, Then contract onboarding is blocked pending sponsor legal review.
external_authorization_required: Sponsor board resolution or delegated-authority approval adopting the exit policy.

related_question_answers.answer: Yes, by a written sponsor-adopted exit policy applied per fund with individual decision records; batch recommendation is deterministic; execution only with recorded sponsor authority.
No statute found restricting fees or timing; sponsor may impose disclosed contractual fees and deadlines but should not make lawful transfer impracticable; disclose in program terms.

corrections_to_prior_records.issue: Correct but incomplete; the permitted-distribution basis is §4966(c)(2)(A)/(C).
corrections_to_prior_records.correction: Add §4966(c)(2)(A) and (C) and note Schedule N for large exits.

exact_question: Confirm provisional decision: During a fund dispute freeze, do fee accruals, investment rebalancing and recurring grants continue?
original_provisional_answer: During a dispute freeze on a fund: fees continue to accrue; investments follow the standing investment policy but no new advisor-directed allocation changes are accepted; recurring and new grants are held; contributions may be accepted; nothing is distributed until the dispute is resolved by the sponsor.
jurisdiction: Sponsor program terms; state UPMIFA (investment duties); federal §4966

authoritative_findings.claim: Sponsors may freeze accounts while account holders are under investigation or subject to court orders; terms do not specify fee or investment treatment during a freeze.
authoritative_findings.pinpoint: Account privilege limitations; EV-E-002 Termination of account privileges

authoritative_findings.claim: Fidelity's Trustees have exclusive ownership and control over all contributed property and earnings.
Institutional funds must be managed in good faith with ordinary prudence and diversified (UPMIFA).
Fees during a freeze are contractual; no law found requiring suspension of accruals.

supporting_interpretation: An advisory dispute contests who may recommend, not the sponsor's ownership; the sponsor's investment duty continues, so investments should stay on the standing policy (including scheduled rebalancing) and fees accrue as the fund is still administered.
competing_interpretation: Recurring grants previously approved could be viewed as already-decided sponsor grants that should continue; but they derive from a contested advisor's standing instruction, so holding is safer. Fee waiver may be appropriate where the sponsor's error caused the dispute.
applicability_to_unbound: Implement a freeze matrix: accrual continues; collection continues; scheduled policy rebalancing continues; advisor-directed allocation changes blocked; recurring and new grants held; contributions accepted (with acknowledgment); outbound transfers held; mandatory/legal holds override.
business_assumptions: Sponsor investment policy defines automatic rebalancing independent of advisor instructions.
Sponsors may waive fees case by case.
recommended_answer: Confirm: fees accrue and are collected (waiver is a separate sponsor decision); investments follow the standing investment policy including scheduled rebalancing; no advisor-directed allocation changes; recurring and new grants held; contributions accepted; no distribution or transfer until the sponsor resolves the dispute or a court orders otherwise.
remaining_uncertainty: Individual sponsor fee agreements may contain waiver commitments.
consequences_if_wrong: Freezing investments could breach prudence duties; continuing recurring grants could pay contested instructions.
conservative_fallback: Hold all outflows; keep accruals; allow only policy rebalancing.
alternative_design: Full freeze (no rebalancing, no accrual): simpler but risks prudence breach and revenue loss.
required_acceptance_criteria: Given a DisputeFreeze, Then grant, recurring grant, transfer and allocation-change commands are rejected with DISPUTE_FREEZE and fee accrual and policy rebalancing jobs still run.
Given a contribution arrives during a freeze, Then it is accepted and acknowledged and the freeze remains.
Given a court order is recorded, Then it overrides the freeze matrix as directed.

related_question_answers.answer: No; fee accrual and collection continue; waiver is a separate sponsor decision recorded with reason.

exact_question: Confirm provisional decision: Legal form of a sponsor-initiated bulk transfer of funds to another sponsor (grant to sponsoring organization vs asset transfer agreement) and ownership of historical records
original_provisional_answer: A sponsor-initiated bulk transfer is a series of per-fund grants to the receiving sponsoring organization (DAF_TRANSFER_OUT), under a master agreement that records each fund's advisory terms. The source sponsor keeps its records; the receiving sponsor gets a reference copy of fund history, with donor notice before personal data is transferred.
jurisdiction: US federal (§4966, Form 990 Schedules I/D/N); state nonprofit corporation/charitable trust law (AG notice for substantially-all-asset transfers, e.g. Cal. Corp. Code §5913); state privacy law for donor data

authoritative_findings.claim: A distribution from a DAF to another DAF or to a 170(b)(1)(A) organization is not a taxable distribution, so per-fund grants to the receiving sponsor are permitted.
Proposed regs define distribution broadly (any transfer, cash or in kind) and keep DAF-to-DAF non-taxable; still proposed as of 2026-11-24.
A transfer exceeding 25% of net assets (or a related series) that is not an ordinary-course grant must be reported on Schedule N Part II.
A California public benefit corporation must give the AG 20 days' notice before transferring all or substantially all assets outside the usual course.
The source sponsor must retain books and records substantiating its receipts, disbursements and §6033 information.
Sponsor-initiated bulk transfers have precedent (BNY Mellon DAF program moved to RCF).

supporting_interpretation: Per-fund grants to the receiving sponsor keep each sponsor's books correct and use the statutory DAF-to-DAF exception; a master agreement documents the receiving sponsor's acceptance and expected advisory terms. The source sponsor keeps its records as custodian; the receiving sponsor needs history only as reference.
competing_interpretation: An assignment of the whole program (asset transfer agreement) could be cleaner for very large exits and may be required by state law where it is a substantially-all-asset disposition; it is still reportable on Schedule N. A master agreement that obliges the receiving sponsor to honor advisory privileges must not give donors legal control.
applicability_to_unbound: Unbound models DAF_TRANSFER_OUT per fund with a master-agreement reference, sponsor authorization separate from donor recommendations, and a size check against net assets (Schedule N flag) and state AG notice flags.
business_assumptions: Most transfers are well under 25% of the source sponsor's net assets.
Donor privacy notices permit sharing fund history with a successor sponsor; otherwise notice/consent is obtained.
recommended_answer: Confirm: per-fund grants (DAF_TRANSFER_OUT) to the receiving sponsoring organization under a master agreement; each fund's transfer is a separate sponsor-authorized distribution with its own record; source sponsor remains records custodian; receiving sponsor gets a reference copy after donor notice. Add: (1) Schedule N flag if the transfer series exceeds 25% of the source's net assets; (2) state AG notice check where the transfer is all or substantially all assets (e.g., CA 20 days) or the sponsor is dissolving; (3) in-kind transfers allowed only where both sponsors agree (Fidelity has made in-kind DAF-to-DAF grants).
remaining_uncertainty: State-by-state AG notice/approval rules not surveyed beyond California; final §4966 regs pending.
consequences_if_wrong: Missed AG notice or Schedule N reporting; disputes over records ownership.
conservative_fallback: Block execution until both sponsors' counsel approve the master agreement and any AG notice period expires.
alternative_design: Whole-program asset transfer agreement: one legal instrument, needs AG review in many states; per-fund grants (recommended): fits existing grant controls and statute.
required_acceptance_criteria: Given a bulk transfer, Then each fund produces a DAF_TRANSFER_OUT record with master-agreement ID and sponsor authorization distinct from any donor recommendation.
Given the cumulative series exceeds 25% of the source sponsor's beginning net assets, Then a Schedule N flag is raised.
Given the source sponsor is a California public benefit corporation transferring substantially all assets, Then execution is blocked until a 20-day AG notice is recorded.
Given fund history is shared, Then donor notice is recorded before the export is released.
external_authorization_required: Executed master agreement between sponsors; board or delegated approval at the source sponsor; state AG notice/approval where the transfer is substantially all assets.

related_question_answers.answer: Per-fund grants to the receiving sponsor under a master agreement; sponsor authorization recorded separately from donor recommendations; execution blocked until the legal form, AG notice (if any) and history-sharing are approved.

corrections_to_prior_records.issue: Correct statute; precise basis is §4966(c)(2)(A) and (C); record omits Schedule N and state AG notice obligations for large transfers.
corrections_to_prior_records.correction: Cite (c)(2)(A),(C); add Schedule N >25% check and state AG notice gate.

exact_question: Confirm provisional decision: After sponsor exit, how long does the platform keep read-only data and backups, and who is records custodian?
original_provisional_answer: After a sponsor exits, the sponsor is the records custodian. The platform keeps a read-only copy for 90 days after the reconciled export is delivered, then deletes it; backups expire on their normal schedule (no more than 35 days later). Legal holds override deletion. The exit certificate lists any residual copies and their expiry.
jurisdiction: US federal (IRC §6001; Treas. Reg. §1.6001-1); state record-retention and privacy law; contract

authoritative_findings.claim: Exempt organizations must keep books showing receipts and disbursements and substantiating §6033 information, retained as long as material to tax administration.
Generally keep records until the statute of limitations runs (3 years after the later of due date or filing), longer for other legal purposes; governance and exemption documents permanently.
The retention duty rests on the exempt organization (sponsor), not on its software provider.

supporting_interpretation: Since the sponsor bears the duty, the sponsor is the custodian; a platform residual copy is a contractual courtesy for export verification. 90 days of read-only access after a verified export is reasonable.
competing_interpretation: Some sponsors may want the platform to hold records for 7 years as an outsourced archive (contractual service); the platform then becomes a records processor with longer obligations.
applicability_to_unbound: Offer exit export with checksum verification, 90-day read-only period, backup expiry ≤35 days after deletion, legal holds override, exit certificate listing residuals. Optionally offer paid long-term archive.
business_assumptions: Sponsor accepts custody of a complete, verified export.
Backups rotate on a ≤35-day schedule.
recommended_answer: Confirm: sponsor is records custodian; platform keeps read-only copy 90 days after the sponsor confirms the reconciled export, then deletes; backups expire ≤35 days later; legal holds override; exit certificate lists residuals. Contract must state that the sponsor is responsible for retaining records for at least the federal limitation period (generally 3 years after the later of the 990 due/filing date; longer for permanent records and state requirements) and that the platform's optional archive service is separate.
remaining_uncertainty: State-specific retention laws and privacy deletion rights not surveyed.
consequences_if_wrong: Sponsor unable to substantiate returns if export incomplete; platform liability if data retained beyond contract.
conservative_fallback: Hold read-only until the sponsor signs export acceptance, however long that takes, with a contractual fee after 90 days.
alternative_design: Paid 7-year archive service: revenue opportunity, longer data exposure.
required_acceptance_criteria: Given a sponsor exits, When the reconciled export is accepted, Then deletion is scheduled for 90 days later and the exit certificate lists backup expiry dates.
Given a legal hold exists, Then deletion is blocked and the certificate reflects the hold.
external_authorization_required: Executed sponsor contract clause on custody, retention and exit.

related_question_answers.answer: Complete verified export; 90-day read-only period at platform cost (longer at sponsor cost); mandatory retention and legal holds override deletion; sponsor retains records per IRC §6001/Reg. §1.6001-1.

corrections_to_prior_records.issue: Cites only internal records; no legal basis.
corrections_to_prior_records.correction: Add 26 USC 6001 and Treas. Reg. §1.6001-1(c),(e); IRS Pub 4221-PC retention guidance.
